data.title: Telogen effluvium — viva
data.summary: Hair & nail disorders · 10 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Telogen effluvium** (Hair & nail disorders)_

**Q1. Define telogen effluvium (TE).**
- Diffuse, non-scarring increased shedding of telogen (club) hairs occurring 2–4 months after a triggering event that pushes many anagen follicles prematurely into telogen; commonest cause of diffuse hair loss in women

**Q2. Describe the causes and types (PYQ).**
- Acute TE (<6 months): high fever (typhoid, dengue, malaria, COVID-19), major surgery, childbirth (post-partum TE — 2–4 months after delivery), crash dieting/protein deficiency, severe emotional stress, haemorrhage, stopping OCPs, drugs (retinoids, anticoagulants, β-blockers, antithyroid, anticonvulsants)
- Chronic TE (>6 months): iron deficiency, thyroid disease, malnutrition (zinc, protein, vitamin D, biotin rarely), chronic illness (SLE, renal/hepatic failure, HIV), idiopathic chronic TE in middle-aged women (thick hair initially)
- Headington's functional types: immediate anagen release, delayed anagen release (post-partum), short anagen, immediate telogen release (minoxidil initiation), delayed telogen release

**Q3. Clinical features.**
- Sudden increase in hair fall (handfuls while combing/washing) with diffuse thinning, especially bitemporal recession; hair pull test positive (>10% club hairs) all over scalp; no scarring, normal scalp
- Club hairs with depigmented bulb seen on pull test

**Q4. Write a short note on anagen effluvium (PYQ).**
- Abrupt cessation of mitotic activity in anagen follicles → tapered, fractured dystrophic hairs shed within days–weeks (1–4 weeks) of insult; ~80–90% of scalp hair lost
- Causes: chemotherapy (commonest), radiation, thallium/arsenic/mercury poisoning, boric acid, colchicine overdose, severe AA, pemphigus, protein malnutrition (kwashiorkor)
- Usually reversible; regrowth may differ in colour/texture; scalp cooling reduces chemotherapy-induced alopecia; topical minoxidil may speed regrowth

**Q5. How do you differentiate TE, AGA and diffuse AA?**
- TE: sudden shedding after trigger, positive pull test diffusely, uniform hair diameter on trichoscopy, many empty follicles/upright regrowing hairs, frontal ≈ occipital density
- AGA: gradual thinning, pattern distribution, hair diameter diversity >20%, frontal < occipital density, pull test usually negative
- Diffuse AA: rapid diffuse loss, exclamation-mark hairs, yellow and black dots, dystrophic anagen hairs on pull test

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Detailed history of triggers 2–4 months earlier; hair pull test, trichogram (telogen >20–25%), trichoscopy
- CBC, serum ferritin, TSH/free T4, vitamin D, B12, zinc, protein/albumin, LFT/RFT, ANA if indicated, VDRL (if moth-eaten), hormonal profile if signs of hyperandrogenism; biopsy for chronic TE vs early AGA

**Q7. Management.**
- Identify and remove/correct the trigger; reassurance — acute TE recovers in 3–6 months; cosmetic improvement takes 12–18 months
- Correct deficiencies: iron (ferritin), vitamin D, protein-rich diet; treat thyroid disease
- Topical minoxidil 2–5% may shorten duration (initial shedding); avoid harsh hair treatments
- Chronic TE: counselling (stable hair density over time), minoxidil, low-dose oral minoxidil

**Q8. What is the hair pull test and how is it interpreted?**
- Grasp ~50–60 hairs near the scalp and pull gently from proximal to distal — >10% (≥6 hairs) extracted indicates active shedding (TE, active alopecia areata, anagen effluvium); club (telogen) roots in TE

**Q9. What is the normal hair cycle?**
- Anagen (growth, 2–6 years, ~85–90% of scalp hairs), catagen (involution, 2–3 weeks, ~1%), telogen (rest, ~3 months, ~10–15%), exogen (shedding) and kenogen (empty follicle); normal loss 50–100 hairs/day

**Q10. What are the mechanisms of TE (Headington's functional types)?**
- Immediate anagen release (fever, drugs, surgery — premature entry into telogen; shedding after 2–3 months), delayed anagen release (post-partum — prolonged anagen then synchronised shedding), short anagen syndrome, immediate telogen release (minoxidil initiation — early shedding of telogen), delayed telogen release (seasonal shedding in animals/ humans)

## Quick spotter facts
- Diffuse shedding 3 months after typhoid/childbirth, positive pull test — telogen effluvium
- Anagen effluvium — chemotherapy, within weeks

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hair loss). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
